subject: Infer time-dependent variance in Gaussian likelihood from data

messages.author: 93bec28a46e3d2d3
messages.subject: Infer time-dependent variance in Gaussian likelihood from data
parts:
Hi,

I am building a prediction model for a temporal trajectory, with lead times 1,2,...T. The variable of interest can be assumed Gaussian where the mean depends on two covariates with an AR(1) structure on the coefficients. As my predictions get more uncertain the longer the lead time, I would like the Gaussian likelihood to have a time-dependent variance. The structure of this might, for instance, be seasonally varying. I would thus like to learn the time-dependent changes in the variance directly from the data. 

Is this possible? 

Thanks,
Thordis

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Infer time-dependent variance in Gaussian likelihood from data
parts:
On 23/10/13 14:04, Thordis Linda Thorarinsdottir wrote:
> I am building a prediction model for a temporal trajectory, with lead
> times 1,2,...T. The variable of interest can be assumed Gaussian where
> the mean depends on two covariates with an AR(1) structure on the
> coefficients. As my predictions get more uncertain the longer the lead
> time, I would like the Gaussian likelihood to have a time-dependent
> variance. The structure of this might, for instance, be seasonally
> varying. I would thus like to learn the time-dependent changes in the
> variance directly from the data.

Hi Thordis!

You're mixing two separate issues here:
1) that predictions get more uncertain with longer lead times is a
direct effect from calculating conditional distributions into the
future, which will automatically have increasing variances.
2) What you seem to be asking about is that you also want increasing
uncertainty due to uncertainty about changes in the model itself.

Issue 1) is automatic, and issue 2) can be done in at least one way:
For 1D spde models (which includes AR(1) and AR(2)-like models), one can
specify a log-linear model for the spde parameters, such as the
variance, allowing for temporal trends in the model parameters, or
seasonal parameter variation based on seasonal covariates.

Finn

parts:
Hi Finn!

Thank you very much for the very quick response! If I understand correctly, I need to move from classic INLA to SPDE-INLA and then I can do what I want :)

Concerning your first comment, this is related to a different issue which took me a while to understand. I am not only interested in a point prediction, or a prediction for the expected value of my variable, I want a full predictive distribution. One thing I really care about is calibration. If I do what the INLA FAQ suggest, I get a very good point prediction, but the predictive distribution is seriously underdispersive as the variance of the likelihood model is not accounted for. That is, I need to do something like the following

rm(list = ls())
library(INLA)
set.seed(7)
m <- 100
coverage <- 0
for(i in 1:m)
  {
    print(i)
    n <- 100
    X <- rnorm(n)
    Y <- X + rnorm(n)
    trueY <-  Y[n]
    Y[n] <- NA
    D <- data.frame(Y = Y, X = X)
    a <- inla(Y~X, data = D, control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE, quantiles = seq(0.01, 0.99, by = 0.01)))
    ind <- sample(1:99, 1000, replace=TRUE)
    mean.sample <- as.numeric(a$summary.fitted.values[n, 3:101])[ind]
    var.sample <- rnorm(1000, mean=0, sd=1/a$summary.hyperpar[1])
    sample <- mean.sample + var.sample
    lower <- quantile(sample, 0.1)
    upper <- quantile(sample, 0.9)
    if(trueY>=lower & trueY<=upper) coverage <- coverage + 1
  }
coverage

This gives me a coverage of approximately 80% for the 80% prediction interval. If I only look at the quantiles of the distribution in summary.fitted.values, I get a coverage of about 20% as that is not the predictive distribution for the missing variable Y[n]. 

All the best,
Thordis

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Infer time-dependent variance in Gaussian likelihood from data
parts:
On 23/10/13 14:32, Thordis Linda Thorarinsdottir wrote:
> Thank you very much for the very quick response! If I understand
> correctly, I need to move from classic INLA to SPDE-INLA and then I can
> do what I want :)

For some of the non-SPDE models it may still be possible to do something
similar, but essentialy: Yes. ;)

> Concerning your first comment, this is related to a different issue
> which took me a while to understand. I am not only interested in a point
> prediction, or a prediction for the expected value of my variable, I
> want a full predictive distribution.

INLA gives you the predictive distribution for the linear predictor in
the model. If you want the predictive distribution for potential
observations from the observation model that needs to be integrated
separately (except for some special cases where the model can be written
on a form that allows inla to do that integration as well) as that in
general can be both discrete and/or otherwise non-Gaussian.

> One thing I really care about is
> calibration. If I do what the INLA FAQ suggest, I get a very good point
> prediction, but the predictive distribution is seriously underdispersive
> as the variance of the likelihood model is not accounted for.

Well, yes, it the correct predictive distribution for a _different_
latent variable than you unobserved future observations, so the coverage
_shouldn't_ match.

> That is, I
> need to do something like the following
<cut>

> This gives me a coverage of approximately 80% for the 80% prediction
> interval. If I only look at the quantiles of the distribution in
> summary.fitted.values, I get a coverage of about 20% as that is not the
> predictive distribution for the missing variable Y[n].

Yes, "fitted.values" refers to the link-function-transformed linear
predictor, so is not comparable to observations (it describes a
parameter, which is usually an expectation, so it may appear to be on
the same scale as the observations, but it doesn't include the
observational variability at all).

There are several functions to produce posterior samples, e.g.
inla.posterior.sample(), which produces predictive samples from
the latent variables and model parameters, which can then be combined
with sampling from the observation likelihood models. This is currently
the only completely general method I know of for doing observation-scale
predictive distributions with INLA.

Finn

Sounds good, but I just wanted to clarify what we're trying to fit.  We would like to fit a model of the form

Y_{it} = X_{it}B_t + e_{it}

B_{1:T} ~ AR(1)

e_{it} ~ N(0, kappa^{-1}_t)

kappa_t ~ Gamma, iid

i = 1, ..., N (around 40)

t = 1, ..., T (around 72)

In other words we just want a separate precision for each timepoint t. Is moving over to the SPDE framework the only way to get that?  Could it be possible to just use separate likelihoods for each time point, but still get the effect of "sharing" information about B_t across these likelihoods?

Hope I haven't increased the amount of confusion.

Alex

Hi

In this formulation then the number of hyperparameters would be
#kappa's, that is around T=72 + a few more. that is to much in practice.
is there any way to say that you have K groups of the 't's so that all
the \kappa's in each group has (about) the same value.

You probably have quite some uncertainty in a potential estimate of all
the \kappa's, so even though it was possible to have one spesific for
each t, their posteriors would likely be hugly overlapping, so in
practice you would not be able to estimate T different ones and you get
only a few possible unique values ?

If you know some of the kappa's relative scaling, that is also easy to
account for.

H

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Infer time-dependent variance in Gaussian likelihood from data
parts:
> Sounds good, but I just wanted to clarify what we're trying to fit. We
> would like to fit a model of the form
>
> Y_{it} = X_{it}B_t + e_{it}
> B_{1:T} ~ AR(1)
> e_{it} ~ N(0, kappa^{-1}_t)
>
> kappa_t ~ Gamma, iid

Now that's a different story, and someone else may need to answer that;
having a separate precision for _each_ timepoint takes this model into
non-latent-Gaussian-land. The SPDE-model can handle things similar to
log(kappa_t) ~ sum_k Z_k(t) w_k
where there is only a small number of temporally varying covariates Z_k,
but your model has n of those, which is typically too much.

Having separate likelihoods has essentially the same problem, in that it
introduces n "hyper"-parameters in the inla model structure, which is
too much.

Finn
